summary: Vint Cerf's notes on how the IMP operating system controlled traffic flow in 1972, based on a BBN meeting. The goals included fewer needless retransmissions under heavy load and keeping reassembly from locking up. It is an informal account, and RFC 449 offers corrections and better references.

plainLanguage.summary: This note describes how IMPs managed message traffic by reserving room, ordering messages, and confirming packet delivery. It is Vint Cerf's account of a meeting, rather than a formal specification.

questions: how did imp flow control reserve buffers
how did imp messages get acknowledged
subtitle: A participant's account of IMP buffer reservations, message ordering and packet acknowledgments.

tldr.problem: The IMP network needed to reduce unnecessary retransmissions, avoid wasted waiting, and prevent traffic from exhausting buffers needed by other work.
tldr.mechanism: IMPs reserve destination buffers before sending longer messages, number messages for ordering, and carry acknowledgments in packets traveling the other way.
tldr.outcome: This RFC records Vint Cerf's understanding of a meeting, and the unit metadata says RFC 449 updates it.

today: The unit metadata says RFC 442 is updated by RFC 449. The text presents one author's understanding of a meeting about the IMP flow-control scheme.

sections.title: What the Flow-Control Scheme Tries to Do
sections.content:
A meeting at BBN described a new flow-control scheme for the IMP operating system. Vint Cerf writes down his understanding of that scheme.

The goals include reducing unnecessary retransmissions under heavy load, avoiding retransmission delays under light load, increasing bandwidth, preventing reassembly lock-up, and controlling traffic from hosts into the network more strictly than the earlier link-blocking method.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme aims to keep network messages moving when traffic is heavy and light. It also tries to stop one kind of traffic from using all available space.

sections.title: Reserving Space Before Sending
sections.content:
A one-packet message itself requests one packet of buffer space. If the destination has room, it replies with a Request for Next Message (RFNM), and the source discards its saved copy. If there is no room, the destination records the request in a first-come-first-served queue and later sends ALL (1); the source then retries the message.

For a multi-packet message, the source pauses the host-to-IMP line after the first full packet arrives without the last-bit flag. It requests space for 8 packets using REQ (8). When the destination has 8 buffers, it replies ALL (8), and the source sends the message. The destination may delay its RFNM until another 8 buffers are available.

The account describes time-outs: a source retries its request after 30 seconds, and an unused reservation is reset after 2 minutes. After receiving an allocation, the source has 125 ms to begin sending at least the first packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending a long message, the source IMP asks the destination to set aside room. The source waits for the destination's reply, then sends the message when that room is ready.

sections.title: Buffer Limits and Message Order
sections.content:
The system has 40 buffers for store-and-forward and reassembly. At most 32 may be assigned to reassembly and at most 24 to 25 to store-and-forward, so neither use can shut out the other.

An IMP may have at most 4 un-RFNMed messages outstanding to each other IMP. IMPs assign 8-bit message numbers and use 2-bit priority numbers for priority messages. Each pair of sites shares one sequence in each direction, treating all hosts on an IMP as one host. This can let a delayed message for one host delay messages for another. The note warns that assigning priority arbitrarily to a short message can make a file arrive out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: Buffer limits leave room for both message forwarding and message reassembly. Numbering helps the receiving IMP restore message order, although a delayed message can hold up traffic for another host at the same site.

sections.title: Acknowledging Packets on IMP Links
sections.content:
Each full-duplex line is treated as two one-way paths. The sender and receiver use ODD/EVEN (OE) bits to track packets. A packet carries a packet OE (POE) bit and an acknowledgment (ACK) bit: the sender sets them from its send and receive state. A matching acknowledgment frees the sender's channel; a packet with an already-seen OE value is discarded as a duplicate.

Instead of separate acknowledgment packets, the new scheme puts ACK bits in packets traveling in the reverse direction. If no real packet is ready, a fake packet carries the acknowledgment. Each send and receive module has 8 OE bits, allowing up to 8 packets to be outstanding. Packets are prioritized for sending, and the note says a 125 ms time-out forces retransmission of old packets when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets carry small flags that tell the other IMP what arrived. This lets the two IMPs confirm delivery using traffic going back the other way, or a small acknowledgment-only packet when needed.
